c.tagline: Tanzania's steamy Indian Ocean metropolis - harbour bustle, Swahili markets, and the gateway to Zanzibar.

taxi.color: no official uniform color; often white or branded
taxi.fareNote: Meters are rare, so agree the fare before you set off, or use app-based Uber or Bolt for transparent, prepaid pricing.

emergency.note: 112 is the general emergency number reachable from any mobile network; 114 reaches police. Private ambulance and medevac services also operate for tourists.

hood_landmark.City Centre / Kivukoni: St Joseph Cathedral Dar es Salaam
hood_landmark.Oyster Bay: Coco Beach Oyster Bay Dar es Salaam

avoid.reason: Petty crime and bag-snatching in the centre; caution at night and on isolated beaches

hood_desc: Dar's downtown core along the harbour front, home to the Askari Monument, St Joseph's Cathedral, the National Museum, and the Zanzibar ferry terminal; central and busy, best for sightseeing and transport links.

An upmarket, leafy peninsula district full of embassies, expat apartments, and the city's best restaurants, cafes, and bars, plus the Slipway waterfront complex; the top pick for dining and nightlife.

A relaxed, upscale seaside neighbourhood along Coco Beach and Toure Drive, with boutique hotels, ocean-view dining, and weekend beach crowds; suits travellers wanting calm and sea breezes near the action.
Dar's frenetic central market district, a maze of stalls and wholesale shops selling everything from spices to textiles; loud, authentic, and best for budget travellers and immersive local shopping.
A laid-back beach suburb reached by the historic ferry or the Kigamboni Bridge, fringed with palm-shaded sands and low-key beach resorts; a quiet escape from the city bustle.
lodging: Hyatt Regency Dar es Salaam, The Kilimanjaro
Protea Hotel by Marriott Dar es Salaam Oyster Bay

water.note: Drink bottled or filtered water; tap water is not potable.

transit.hours: DART buses and daladalas generally run about 5am-11pm with limited late-night service; ride-hailing apps operate 24/7 and are the recommended option after dark.
transit.note: Traffic congestion is severe at peak hours. The DART bus rapid transit (Mwendokasi) runs on dedicated lanes, cheap daladala minibuses cover everywhere else, and ferries cross to Kigamboni and to Zanzibar; many visitors rely on Uber or Bolt for comfort.
transit.pay: DART fares use a smart card or cash at station gates; daladalas are paid in cash to the conductor. Ferry and Zanzibar tickets are bought at the terminal counters.

ferry: Zanzibar fast ferries (Azam Marine / Zan Fast)
train: Tanzania SGR (Standard Gauge Railway to Morogoro / Dodoma)

transit.m: Daladala minibus toward the city centre (~45-75 min)
Taxi or ride-hail to the city centre (30-45 min)

tip.r: Around 10% at tourist restaurants if no service charge is added; small tips for guides, drivers, and hotel staff are appreciated.

food.name: Nyama choma with ugali
food.desc: Charcoal-grilled beef or goat served with ugali, a stiff maize meal, and kachumbari salad; Tanzania's signature communal meal.

places.name: Sanaa Restaurant
places.note: Relaxed garden grill known for well-spiced roast meats served with fresh hot ugali.

places.name: Mamboz Corner BBQ
places.note: Long-running open-air street grill in the old town, packed with charcoal roasts every night.

places.name: Chef's Pride
places.note: Budget local institution serving Tanzanian staples from breakfast through to late evening.

food.name: Mishkaki
food.desc: Marinated beef or goat skewers grilled over charcoal, brushed with chilli and lime and eaten straight off the stick at street grills.

places.name: Mamboz Corner BBQ
places.note: The city's best known skewer stop; order by the stick with chilli sauce and naan.

places.name: Samaki Samaki
places.note: Buzzy African-fusion spot where grilled beef skewers are a standing menu highlight.

places.name: Chef's Pride
places.note: Cheap, reliable mishkaki alongside a broad menu of Swahili home cooking.

food.name: Zanzibar mix (urojo)
food.desc: Tangy Zanzibari soup of potato, bhajia, coconut chutney and crisps in a turmeric broth; a coastal snack that crossed to the mainland.

places.name: Coco Beach food stalls
places.note: Evening beachfront stalls ladling Zanzibari mix and grilled snacks to order.

places.name: Kariakoo Market food stalls
places.note: Dar's biggest market; the surrounding lanes are wall-to-wall cheap Swahili street food.

places.name: Chef's Pride
places.note: Sit-down version of the coastal classics for anyone wary of street stalls.

food.name: Chipsi mayai
food.desc: Tanzania's beloved chip omelette: hot fries folded into egg and fried flat, served with kachumbari and fiery pili pili sauce.

places.name: Mamboz Corner BBQ
places.note: Street-side griddles turning out chip omelettes alongside the charcoal grills.

places.name: Coco Beach food stalls
places.note: Cooked to order at sunset stalls along the Msasani seafront promenade.

places.name: Chef's Pride
places.note: Popular budget kitchen where chipsi mayai is an all-day order.

food.name: Wali wa nazi na samaki
food.desc: Coconut rice with grilled or curried Indian Ocean fish, a Swahili coast staple perfumed with tamarind, cumin and cardamom.

places.name: Kivukoni Fish Market
places.note: Waterfront market where the morning catch is fried or grilled at stalls behind the auction hall.

places.name: Samaki Samaki
places.note: Seafood-led kitchen with coconut-rich Swahili preparations and creative fish plates.

places.name: Chef's Pride
places.note: Daily coconut rice and fish plates at local prices.

food.name: Ndizi nyama
food.desc: Green plantains simmered with beef in a rich, lightly spiced broth; northern comfort food now found on menus right across the city.

places.name: Chef's Pride
places.note: Signature plate here, usually eaten with matembele sweet potato greens.

places.name: Sanaa Restaurant
places.note: Traditional stews served in a friendly garden dining room.

places.name: Kariakoo Market food stalls
places.note: Lunch canteens around the market serve it by the plate at market prices.

food.name: Madafu (fresh coconut water)
food.desc: Green coconuts chopped open on the spot and drunk through a straw, with the soft jelly scooped out afterwards; sold all along the coast road.

places.name: Coco Beach promenade vendors
places.note: Carts line the seafront walk; the vendor splits the shell for the jelly after you drink.

places.name: Kivukoni Fish Market
places.note: Coconut sellers work the waterfront alongside the fish traders.

places.name: Kariakoo Market
places.note: Cheapest madafu in the city, sold by the barrowload at the market edges.

food.name: Kilimanjaro and Safari lager
food.desc: Tanzania's two big local beers, poured ice cold; Konyagi, a local sugarcane spirit, is the usual alternative for a nightcap.

places.name: Samaki Samaki
places.note: Late-night bar crowd, cold local beer and creative cocktails using Konyagi.

places.name: The Slipway
places.note: Waterfront complex of bars and terraces with sunset views over the peninsula.

places.name: Sanaa Restaurant
places.note: Cold beers to go with the charcoal grill in an easy garden setting.

landmarks: St. Joseph's Metropolitan Cathedral
This twin-spired Gothic-style Catholic cathedral, built by German missionaries in the early 1900s, is one of the most photographed waterfront landmarks in the city.
Askari Monument
This bronze statue honoring African soldiers who fought in World War I stands at the historic heart of downtown Dar es Salaam.
Azania Front Lutheran Church
A striking red-roofed German colonial church right on the harbor, offering one of the most iconic waterfront silhouettes in the city.
National Museum of Tanzania
Home to important hominid fossil discoveries and Tanzania's cultural history, this museum is a must for understanding the country's deep heritage.
Kariakoo Market
A sprawling, colorful, and chaotic market that captures the authentic pulse of everyday Dar es Salaam life.
Village Museum (Makumbusho)
An open-air museum showcasing traditional homesteads from across Tanzania's many ethnic groups, offering a vivid cultural photo opportunity.
Bongoyo Island
A short boat ride from the city, this pristine marine-reserve island offers postcard-perfect white sand beaches and coral reefs.
Coco Beach (Oyster Bay)
The city's liveliest beach promenade, especially at sunset, packed with locals, street food, and views over the Indian Ocean.
Kigamboni Ferry Crossing
This iconic harbor ferry crossing offers dramatic skyline views of the city's port and downtown skyline.
Msasani Slipway
A popular waterfront shopping and dining complex with a lively craft market and scenic ocean views over Msasani Bay.

intl.to: Kapiri Mposhi (Zambia) - the TAZARA line, ~46 hr

train.note: Dar es Salaam has one of Africa's great international trains: the TAZARA runs twice a week to Kapiri Mposhi in Zambia, a two-day journey through the Selous game reserve where you may see wildlife from the window. It departs from its own terminal south-west of the centre, separate from the main station. Domestically, the new SGR electric trains to Dodoma and Morogoro are fast and modern, with the line extending toward Mwanza. Book TRC tickets online or at the station.

intl.to: Nairobi & Mombasa (Kenya) - via the Namanga or Lunga Lunga border

intl.op: Taqwa / Kobil / regional operators — tickets at the Magufuli bus terminal

bus.note: Long-distance coaches use the Magufuli (Mbezi) terminal about 20 km from the centre, which catches people out - allow an hour to reach it. Nairobi takes about 12-14 hours via Namanga, Arusha 8-10. Carry your passport; note that Tanzania is not part of the East Africa Tourist Visa, so a separate visa is needed. Book through the operators or at the terminal.

intl.to: Zanzibar - Stone Town (Tanzania) - ~2 hr fast catamaran

ferry.note: There is no international sailing from Dar es Salaam, but the Zanzibar catamarans are among the busiest passenger routes in East Africa, running several times a day from the ferry terminal on Kivukoni Front in the middle of the city. Note that Zanzibar has its own immigration formalities, so carry your passport even though it is domestic travel. Book online or at the terminal; sailings can be rough during the monsoon.

half.name: Bagamoyo
half.blurb: Former 19th-century trading port with a UNESCO-listed stone town, the Kaole ruins, and a colonial-era Catholic mission.

full.name: Zanzibar (Stone Town)
full.blurb: Spice island reached by fast ferry, with a UNESCO-listed old town of carved wooden doors and narrow winding lanes.

full.name: Saadani National Park
full.blurb: Tanzania's only park where the beach meets the bush, with game drives and a boat safari along the Wami River.
